1.36.m: Pulastya said: / Then those gods departed in many celestial chariots at that time, / and Rāma also quickly followed to the penance grove of the pot-born sage.
[Rāma thought:] "A return has been spoken of by that lord, 'Perform the rites,' / who had previously come to the assembly to see me.
Therefore, by the command of the gods, for the sake of their purpose, / having gone I shall see that great sage, worshipped by gods and Dānavas.
And pleased, that best of beings will personally give me instruction, / by which I shall never again become sorrowful in this mortal world.
Daśaratha is my father, and Kausalyā my mother; / I was born in the Solar dynasty; nevertheless, I am very sorrowful thus.
At the time of taking the kingdom, dwelling in the forest took place with my wife and younger brother; / and the abduction of my wife was also carried out by Rāvaṇa.
Yet, crossing the great ocean without allies, / besieging that entire city and causing the destruction of his family,
Sītā was seen and abandoned by me before the gods at that time. / They declared to me that she was pure, and so Sītā was brought home by me
with affection, [yet] sent away due to the talk of the people. / That noble lady lives in the forest, and I dwell in the city.
I was born in the highest family; I am the highest among archers; / yet I have met with the highest sorrow, and my heart does not burst!
Surely I was fashioned by the Creator out of the essence of adamant. / Now, by order of the Brahmin, I wander upon the surface of the earth.
That sinful Śūdra engaged in asceticism has been struck down by me. / By the word of the gods, however, my breath has settled again in my heart.
I shall see that venerable sage, devoted to the welfare of this world; / once he is seen, my sorrow will quickly go to destruction in the same way.
Just as frost dissolves with the rising of the thousand-rayed sun, / so the arrival of my sorrow will completely go to destruction."
Seeing the gods arrived, the venerable ṛṣi Agastya, / taking guest-water, worshipped all of them with great pleasure.
Receiving that worship and conversing with the great sage, / they, accompanied by their followers, then joyfully went to the vault of heaven.
When they had gone, Kākutstha, having descended from the Puṣpaka, / arrived to pay homage to that excellent ṛṣi Agastya.
The king said: / "I am the son of Daśaratha, come indeed to pay homage to you, / O best of sages! Look [upon me] with a gentle eye.
Having seen you, I become cleansed of sin here, without doubt." / Having spoken this much and saluted the sage again and again,
[he inquired about] the welfare of his group of servants, the deer, and his son: / "Desiring the sight of the venerable lord, I have come here after slaying the Śūdra."
Agastya said: / "Welcome to you, O best of Raghu's line, eternal one adored by the world! / From seeing you, O descendant of Kakutstha, I, together with the sages, have become purified."
For your sake, O tiger among the Raghus, accept the guest-water, O one of great splendor! / Welcome, O tiger among men! By good fortune you have arrived, O slayer of foes!
For you are constantly held in high esteem on account of many excellent virtues; / therefore you are indeed worthy of worship, constantly dwelling in my heart.
The gods indeed speak of you as having arrived after slaying the Śūdra, / and by you, through righteousness, the son of the Brahmin has been brought to life.
Dwell here, O venerable Rāghava, in my presence; / at dawn you shall depart for Ayodhyā in the Puṣpaka, O wise one!
And this ornament, gentle one, beautifully fashioned by Viśvakarman, / divine, shining with its own brilliance with a divine form—
accept it, O king of kings, and do what is pleasing to me, O Rāghava! / For great fruit is said to come from the giving away of what has been acquired."

For you are able to protect even the foremost gods led by Indra;
therefore, I shall give it to you according to the rules: receive it, O bull among men!

Then the mighty-armed one, the great car-warrior of the Ikṣvākus,
folding his hands, spoke to the best of sages, remembering his own dharma:

“Indeed, acceptance of gifts from you, O blessed one, is condemned here.
How can an accepting [of a gift] be taken by a knowing kṣatriya, O brahmin?

You ought to tell me: when given by a brahmin,
I have sons, I have a household, and I am capable, O great sage;

and I am not overwhelmed by distress—how is acceptance of gifts to be taken?
My wife was lost long ago, and there is no other for me.

I would merely become a partaker in sin here, without doubt.
Even a kṣatriya, having reached a dire condition, becoming a receiver of gifts,

in doing so incurs no sin; Manu alone is the authority here.
Aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son—

even after doing a hundred improper deeds, they must be supported: so Manu declared.
I will not receive the gift offered by you, O brahmin seer;
nor should any anger indeed be directed at me by you, who are revered by the gods.”

Agastya said:
“There is no sin in the acceptance of gifts when it is taken by kings, O king.
You indeed are able to save even the three worlds, O Rāghava.

Deliver the brahmin, O Rāma, especially an ascetic!
Therefore I shall give it to you according to the rules: receive it, O lord of men!”

Rāma said:
“How can an accepting [of a gift] be taken by a knowing kṣatriya, O brahmin,
when it is given by a brahmin? You ought to tell me that.”

Agastya said:
“There was in the ancient Kṛta age, purified by Brahmā, O Rāma,
a time when all subjects were kingless, and Śatakratu was [king] of the gods.

Those subjects approached the lord of the gods for the sake of a king:
‘The gods have a king, the lord of gods, Śatakratu.

Now make a king among us, O lord of the worlds, for our welfare,
in whom men, rendering homage, may enjoy the earth.’

Then Brahmā, the best of the gods, having summoned the world-protectors
along with Indra, said to them all: ‘Let a share of your splendor be united here.’

Then the world-protectors each gave a fourth part from their own splendor,
and then imperishable Brahmā [gave as well], whence the imperishable king was born.

Brahmā joined that portion of the world-protectors into a man;
then the king, wise in [maintaining] welfare, belonged to those subjects.

There, by the portion of Indra, the king issues commands to all;
and by the portion of Varuṇa, he nourishes all embodied beings.

Likewise, by the portion of Kubera, the king distributes wealth;
and that share in the king which belongs to Yama—by it he punishes the subjects.

And there, by the portion of Indra, you are a king, O best of the Raghus;
receive the ornament for the sake of my deliverance, O lord!”

Then Rāma accepted from the hand of the great-souled sage
the wonderful divine ornament, blazing as it were like the sun.

Then, having received it from Agastya, Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
gazed upon it for a long time, examining it again and again.

Variegated pearls, the size of myrobalan fruits,
set in Jambūnada gold, alongside diamonds, corals, and sapphires,

with rubies, together with hessonites, cat's-eyes, and topazes,
firmly fastened, well proportioned, well made by Viśvakarman.

Seeing it, filled with delight, he further reflected on this:
‘No such jewels have ever been seen by me,

fitted with embellishments and equal in value to the earth;
not even in Vibhīṣaṇa’s Laṅkā were they seen by me before.’
Considering this in his mind, Rāghava then began / to ask that sage again about the coming of that divine one.

“This is most wondrous, O holy one, and unobtainable for earthly kings;
how was it obtained by the blessed one, or from where, and by whom was it fashioned?

Driven by curiosity, I ask you, O large-minded one:
when a gem is placed in the palm, if [only] the center of the hand is illuminated,

one should know it to be inferior, condemned in all the treatises;
that which illuminates the directions is middling, O best of sages;

that which rises upward in three crests is declared to be superior.
These superior varieties have indeed been proclaimed by the ṛṣis.

Indeed, the blessed one is a treasure-house of many divine wonders.”
While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, the sage then spoke these words:

Agastya said:
“Listen, O Rāma, to the great event that took place in the ancient Tretā age,
[and] what I saw in the forest when the Dvāpara age had arrived.

Learn of the wonder, O mighty-armed son of the Raghus!
Formerly, in the Tretā age, there was a vast forest,

extending a hundred yojanas all around, devoid of deer and tigers.
In that deserted forest, desiring to perform supreme austerities,

I arrived, O gentle one, to enter that forest.
Now, the interior of that forest was constantly supplied with roots and fruits,

with vegetables of many forms and various kinds in beautiful woods.
In the middle of that forest, extending five yojanas in length,

crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, adorned with cakravāka birds,
there I saw a wonder: an exceedingly beautiful lake,

crowded with crawling turtles, accompanied by flocks of rows of herons.
Long ago I went near that lake to perform austerities,

having reached that sacred place entirely devoid of violence;
there I dwelt for a summer night, O bull among men.

Rising early at dawn, I approached that lake;
then I saw a corpse, untouched by decay anywhere,

lying not very far from the lake with supreme beauty.
Reflecting on its meaning for a moment, O Rāghava:

‘On its shore there is indeed no living creature; or who is this best of gods?
Or is he a sage, or a king? Where is a sage or a king here?

Or perhaps he is the son of a king, whose origin was made thus;
whether he died during the elapsed day, or in the night, or in the morning,

the mystery of this lake must certainly be known by me.’
While I remained thus thinking, O best of the Raghus,

then after a moment I saw a divine, wonderfully visible
and exceedingly splendid aerial chariot, drawn by swans and swift as thought.

There before it, in the aerial chariot, a thousand apsarases, O king,
and as many Gandharvas delighted an excellent man.

They were singing divine songs, and others were playing musical instruments;
then I saw the man descending from that aerial chariot,

and, having bathed, eating the flesh of the corpse, O scion of Raghu's line!
Then, having eaten the very plump flesh as much as he desired,

and stepping down into the lake, he quickly ascended to heaven again.
To him, resembling a god and endowed with supreme splendor, [I said]:

‘O celestial one, O fortunate one, I ask you: how is this?
Repugnant is your food, yet this supreme state is yours!

If this is not a secret of yours, may you tell it to me today;
out of curiosity I wish to hear what this supreme matter is.

Who are you? Tell me, dispelling doubt! And this food is condemned;
by you this is eaten, O gentle one. For what reason, and where do you dwell?

Whose is this lordly condition, fashioned in the form of a corpse?
And why [is there this] blameworthy food? I wish to hear according to truth.’”
Hearing my speech there, O Rāma, best of the virtuous, / that denizen of heaven replied with folded hands, O descendant of Raghu:
"Listen now to what happened to me, born of pleasure and pain; / for desire leads to transgression. Listen to what you ask, O twice-born!
Long ago, my father was the king of Vidarbha, renowned for great fame, / known as Vāsudeva, righteous throughout the three worlds.
Two sons were born to him, O brahmin, by two wives: / I was known as Śveta, and the younger was Suratha.
When our father passed away, the citizens consecrated me; / there I ruled the kingdom, devoted to righteousness.
"In this manner many thousands of years passed by, / as I ruled the kingdom and protected my subjects.
Through a certain cause, O best of the twice-born, filled with dispassion / and fixing death in my heart, I went to an ascetic grove.
I entered this delightful forest, totally devoid of birds, / to undertake ascetic penance near this very lake.
Having anointed my brother Suratha as king over the kingdom, / I came to this lake and performed extremely severe austerities.
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years in the great forest, / I reached that auspicious realm, the disease-free world of Brahmā.
Yet, though residing in heaven, O brāhmaṇa, O best of the twice-born, hunger and thirst / tormented me greatly, and my senses were in agony.
Then I said to the Grandfather, the foremost in the three worlds: / 'O Lord, this heavenly world is free from hunger and thirst.
Of what deed is this the ripening, by which hunger and thirst afflict me? / And what is my food, O Lord? Tell me, glorious Grandfather!'
Then the Grandfather, meditating deeply for a long time, O great sage, / spoke these words to me: 'There is no food except that which is born of your own body.
"Except for yourself, eat your own flesh constantly; / for you nourished your own body while performing excellent asceticism."
What is not given does not arise, dear Śveta; see this on the earth: / formerly, not even an alms-portion was given to a living creature begging insistently,
nor was it given at home to a guest, due to delusion and error. / Therefore, even though you have gone to heaven, you now have hunger and thirst.
Eat your own unexcelled body, well-nourished by foods, / O best of kings; that will bring you satisfaction.'
Being addressed thus, I then said to the god Brahmā: / 'And when my own body has been eaten, I shall have nothing else, O Lord.
The hunger of this body cannot be removed without food. / If I eat what is inexhaustible, O god, it is not pleasing to me.'
Then Brahmā spoke again: 'Your body has been made inexhaustible; / day by day, O Śveta, your corpse will become plump.
Eat your own flesh, O king, until a full hundred years have passed. / When the great ascetic Agastya comes to the Śveta forest,
the Lord, who is extremely invincible, will release you from your distress. / For he is capable of delivering even the gods and asuras along with Indra.
Why speak of this vile food of yours, O royal sage? / A great service to the gods was performed by that great-souled one:
He made the ocean waterless, and the Dānavas were struck down; / and the Vindhya mountain, which was expanding out of hatred for the sun, was restrained.
And this earth, sinking down, was weighed down by heaviness; / the southern quarter rose to the sky, and the three worlds became uneven.
Going together with the gods, he was sent by me to the southern quarter: / “Make the world level, O fortunate one, by your heaviness!”
And so, by that sage staying there, the entire earth was made level / by the sage, O best of kings; and so it is seen even today.'
Having heard the words of the Lord, the God of gods, / I consumed this vile food, my own unexcelled body.
Today a full hundred years of this vile eating have ended; / it does not diminish, O brāhmaṇa, and my satisfaction is supreme.
Tormented by distress, I think of that sage day and night: / 'When indeed will that sage grant me his sight in the forest?'
As I was thus thinking, a hundred years passed here. / That sage Agastya will surely be my refuge, O brāhmaṇa;
there will be no refuge for me except the pot-born twice-born.' / Hearing him speak thus, O Rāma, and seeing that vile food,
filled with supreme compassion, [I thought regarding] that heaven-dwelling king: / 'I shall make nectar his food, and destroy this vile [sustenance]!'
Thinking thus, I said to him: 'What will Agastya do? / I shall destroy this vile [food], O intelligent one!
Ask for whatever is desired from me that brings supreme pleasure to your mind.' / Then that dweller of heaven said to me: 'How can the word of Brahmā
"O sage, it is possible for me to do it, and no other will deliver [us], / except indeed that pot-born one who arose from Mitra and Varuṇa.
Even though unasked by me, O brāhmaṇa, the Grandfather spoke thus.' / To Śveta who was speaking thus, I said: 'I am he!
I have arrived through your good fortune; you have seen me, there is no doubt of this.' / Then that dweller of heaven, recognizing me, fell prostrate on the ground.
Raising him up, O Rāma, I said: 'What shall I do for you?' / The king said: / 'Deliver me today, O brāhmaṇa, from this vile food, from this sin,
By which an imperishable world, heaven, will be mine through your deed." / Then indeed a gift was given by the king adored by the world.
'May you favor me; please accept this gift.'
My mind was set on delivering him, not out of greed, O delight of the Raghu lineage! / When the ornament was taken, O Rāma, and had reached my hand, then
the previous human body of that king was destroyed. / And when the body was dissolved, the royal sage, with supreme joy,
dismissed by me, went again to the third heaven in a celestial chariot. / By him, who was equal to Indra, this auspicious ornament was given to me.
On that occasion, O descendant of Kakutstha, it was given by him of wonderful deeds; / then Śveta, the king of Vidarbha, became free from sin."

1.37.m: Pulastya said: / Hearing those most wonderful words, the delight of the Raghu lineage, / out of respect and wonder, began to ask further.
Rāma said: / "O venerable one, that dreadful forest where he performed austerities, / Śveta, the king of Vidarbha—how did that wonderful thing occur?
That forest was rugged, desolate, and devoid of wild animals; / how did the king enter it to undertake austerities? Tell me, O great sage!
How did it become uninhabited by humans for a hundred yojanas all around? / How did you enter it, and for what purpose? Tell me that!"
Agastya said: / "Formerly in the Kṛta age there was a king, Manu, the lord who wielded the rod of punishment. / Then he had a son named Ikṣvāku of boundless splendor.
Placing that eldest son, who was esteemed on earth, on the throne, / he said: 'Become the king of the royal dynasties on the earth.'
'So be it,' was the promise made by the son to the father, O descendant of Raghu. / Then, highly delighted, he spoke to him again:
'I am pleased with this most noble deed, without doubt; / protect the people with the rod of punishment, and do not punish without cause.
The punishment that is inflicted on offenders here by men— / that punishment, administered according to rule, leads the ruler to heaven.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, be diligent with the rod of punishment, my son! / Thus your supreme dharma in the world will be fulfilled.'
Having thus instructed his son at length through meditation, / Manu, delighted, went to the third heaven, the incomparable world of Brahmā.
He became deeply anxious, thinking: 'How shall I produce sons?' / Through many different rites, he was blessed with sons.
He pleased the ancestors with sons equal to the sons of gods. / The best of all of them was the youngest, O delight of the Raghu lineage,
heroic, educated, and venerable by the honor of the people. / The wise father then gave him the name Daṇḍa.
Foreseeing the coming stroke of the rod upon his body, / and contemplating that dreadful fault of his son, O Rāghava,
the lord gave him a kingdom between the Vindhya and Nīla mountains; / and he, Daṇḍa, became king there on the charming summit of a mountain.
An incomparable city was founded by him as a residence, / and the name of that city was personally called Madhumatta.
Enriched by that country, the valiant king took up residence there; / thus with his royal priest the king ruled that kingdom,
rejoicing and teeming with flourishing subjects, like the king of the gods in heaven. / Then that Daṇḍa, O Kākutstha, for an assembly of many years,
the righteous-minded one, ruled the kingdom freed of all thorns. / Then, at a certain time, the king came to the hermitage of the Bhārgava,
which was delightful, during the charming month of Caitra. / There Daṇḍa saw the daughter of the Bhārgava, peerless on earth in beauty,
wandering in a region of the forest, peerless, / tall, plump, of youthful dark complexion, with a lovely face like the moon,
with a fine nose, beautiful in all limbs, with full and swelling breasts, / slender at the waist and broad in the hips; seeing her, he felt delight.
Dressed in a single garment, alone in the forest, standing in her first youth, / seeing her, unrighteously, he was tormented by the arrows of the Bodiless One.
Approaching the maiden, who was resting well, he spoke these words: / 'From where do you come, O fair-hipped one, and whose are you, O beautiful woman?
Tormented by the Bodiless One, I ask you, O beautiful woman; / my mind has been stolen by you, O lovely one, at the mere sight of you.
This charming face of yours captivates the minds of sages; / if I do not obtain you for enjoyment, consider me dead.
My life-breaths have been stolen by you; grant me life, O fair-eyed one! / I am your slave, O woman of lovely limbs; accept me, your devotee, O beautiful woman!'
To him who spoke in this way, maddened by passion and lustful, / the daughter of the Bhārgava replied with humble words to the king:
'Know me as the eldest daughter of the Bhārgava, Śukra of untiring deeds, / who dwells in the hermitage; Araja is my name, O lord of kings.
Śukra is my father, O lord of kings, and you are a pupil of that great soul; / therefore, according to dharma, I am your sister, O prince.
You ought not to utter such words, O earthly king; / I am to be protected by you at all times, even from other wicked persons.
My father is wrathful and fierce; he would reduce you to ashes. / Or, if you make a union by kingly law, doing so by force,
ask my father through an act sanctioned by righteousness; / woo me from my father of great splendor, O best of kings!
Otherwise, vast and dreadful sorrow will surely be yours; / for my father, if angered, would burn up the entire three worlds.'
Then, having heard that very terrible and dire misfortune, / Daṇḍa, maddened with passion, bowed his head again and answered:
'Grant your favor, O fair-hipped woman, to one maddened by passion, O desirable one! / My life-breaths, restrained by you, are dispersing, O lovely-faced one.
Having obtained you, let there be enmity for me here, or even a greater slaughter! / Accept me, your devotee, O timid woman; for my devotion to you is supreme.'
Having spoken thus, seizing that maiden by force with one arm, / she was stripped of her clothes with the king's other hand.
Clasping limb to limb and placing his mouth against her mouth, / he proceeded at his desire to intercourse with her as she struggled.
Having committed that very dreadful and horrific outrage, / Daṇḍa went quickly to his city like an elephant maddened with rut.
The daughter of the Bhārgava, weeping miserably not far from the hermitage, / agitated, awaited her father, who was equal to a god.
After a moment, having performed his ablutions, the divine sage of boundless splendor, / afflicted with hunger, returned to his hermitage surrounded by his disciples.
He saw the wretched Araja covered all over with dust, / like the moonlight overwhelmed by clouds, utterly defeated.
Anger arose in that great soul afflicted with hunger; / as if burning the three worlds, he addressed those disciples:
'Behold the catastrophe, resembling a blazing flame of fire, / of the perverse Daṇḍa, who lacks foresight,
whereby he has met destruction and ruin along with his followers, without doubt! / For he has touched the spark of a blazing sacrificial fire here.
Since he has committed such an evil deed, equal to a dire sin, / therefore that fool shall receive a dreadful shower of dust.
The bad king, together with his realm, his servants, army, and mounts, / practicing evil deeds, that wicked-minded one shall meet his death.
Over a hundred leagues all around, the territory of that wicked-minded one / let Pākaśāsana sweep with a great rain of dust!
All creatures that are here, moving and unmoving, / the destruction of them all shall happen swiftly by the rain of dust.
As far as the realm of Daṇḍa extends, together with the forests and hermitages, / there shall suddenly be a rain of dust for seven nights.'
Having spoken thus, burning with anger, he said to the people / residing in that hermitage: "Let it remain at the border of the realm!"
As soon as Uśanas had spoken, the people of the hermitage and dwellings / quickly made their abode outside that territory.
Having addressed that company of sages thus, he said this to Arajā: / 'Live in the hermitage, O foolish girl, concentrated in mind.
This hermitage, extending for a league, of charming splendor— / free from passion, stay free from defilement here for a hundred years of time.'
Hearing the command of the brahmin sage, Arajā, daughter of the Bhārgava, / deeply distressed, then said to her father, the Bhārgava: 'So be it.'
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Bhṛgu set out for another dwelling from there. / Within seven days it was reduced to ashes, just as was stated by the expounder of the Veda.
Therefore, the realm of Daṇḍa on the Vindhya mountain, O mortal, / was cursed by Uśanas, O Rāma, when that outrage was committed.
From that time forth, O Kākutstha, it has been called the Daṇḍaka forest. / All this has been narrated to you, which you asked me, O Rāghava.
O hero, the time to perform the twilight worship is slipping away; / these great sages, O Rāma, with filled jars on all sides,
Having offered water, O tiger among men, they worship the Sun / with hymns practiced by all the sages and composed by Brahmā and the others.
"The Sun has set, O Rāma; go and touch water." / Accepting the word of the sage, Rāma [went] to attend the evening twilight.
Rāma, that descendant of Raghu, approached that holy lake. / Then in that forest region, delightful and adorned with trees,
by a holy river on the excellent mountain, decorated with hundreds of cuckoos, / an orchard echoing with the sounds of various birds and teeming with various wild animals,
Teeming with lions and tigers, and crowded with various twice-born birds, / a vulture and an owl had lived abroad there for many hosts of years.
Then the vulture, determined upon sin, claiming, “This is mine,” / seized the owl’s dwelling and quarrelled with him.
“Rāma of lotus eyes is king of the whole world; / let the two of us quickly go to him, [to determine] whose dwelling this must be.”
The vulture and the owl approached, filled with anger and indignation; / with minds perturbed by strife, they went quickly to Rāma.
Hating one another, they nonetheless touched his feet; / and seeing the chief of the Raghus, the vulture spoke these words:
“I consider you foremost among gods and demons; / superior even to Bṛhaspati and Śukra, great in intellect,
knowing the higher and lower natures of beings, a second Indra among mortals, / hard to behold like the sun, and like the Himālaya in majesty,
and you are an ocean in profundity, for you are indeed Yama, guardian of the world; / in patience you are equal to the earth, and in swiftness like the wind,
an elder endowed with all virtues, an embodiment of Viṣṇu, O Rāghava, / intolerant [of injustice], invincible, victorious, having traversed the full rules of all missiles.
Listen, O lord of gods, O bull among men, to my petition: / by the strength of my own arms, O lord, my dwelling was made long ago.
The owl is seizing it, O king, right before you; / such is his wicked conduct, a transgressor of your command, O king!
With capital punishment, O Rāma, you ought to punish him.” / When this had been said by the vulture, the owl spoke these words:
“Hear my petition with an attentive mind, O divine king: / from Soma, from Indra, from Sūrya, from the giver of wealth, and from Yama,
a king is indeed born, O Rāma, and is only somewhat human; / but you are a god composed of all, devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
You are said to be Soma, O king, when an affair is properly weighed; / and you protect [subjects] well from torments, for you dispel darkness.
Because you punish subjects for fault and take away the fear of sin, / and because you are a giver, a striker, and a protector, you are indeed an Indra to us.
You are unassailable among all beings, and considered like fire in your splendour; / you continually burn wicked people; therefore, O Rāma, you are the sun.
You are manifestly equal to the lord of wealth, or even greater than the giver of wealth; / your wife, Śrī, is ever subject to your heart, O best of kings.
By his treasury he is the giver of wealth, and so are you, O lord; / you are impartial toward all beings, moving and unmoving.
Your gaze falls equally all around upon foe and friend, O Rāghava; / your rule is ever righteous, through the procedural courses of legal administration.
He with whom you are angry, O Rāma, is called dead; / therefore, O king, you are celebrated in song as Yama.
And that human nature which is yours, O best of kings, / makes you a king devoted to benevolence, filled with compassion for all.
The king is indeed the strength of the weak and the helpless; / he is an eye to the sightless, and an intellect to the dull-witted.
You are our protector too; let my [plea] be heard, O righteous one; / you must not think of us merely as birds.
He who is our lord, the king of birds, is your servant; / and we are not without a master in your presence, O lord.
By you alone was the fourfold assembly of living beings created of old; / but this vulture, entering my dwelling, oppresses me, O king.
You alone are the punisher among gods and humans, O bull among men.” / Hearing this, Rāma himself summoned his ministers:
Dṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, Rāṣṭravardhana, / Aśoka, Dharmapāla, and the mighty Sumantra.
These were the ministers of Rāma and of King Daśaratha, / endowed with policy, high-souled, skilled in all scriptures,
well-composed, of noble birth, and proficient in guidance and counsel. / Having summoned them, that righteous-souled one descended from the Puṣpaka,
and the best of Raghus questioned the vulture and the owl who were arguing: / “For how many years, vulture, has this dwelling been yours?
Tell me this with curiosity, if you truly know.” / Hearing these words, the vulture spoke to the waiting Rāghava:
“This earth, O Rāma, was covered with tall, many-armed humans / all over; since then it has been my home.”
The owl, however, said to Rāma: “Ever since the earth, / O king, was adorned with trees, since then it has been my home.”
Hearing this, Rāma spoke to the assembly-members: / “That is not an assembly where there are no elders; they are not elders who do not speak dharma;
that is not dharma where there is no truth; that is not truth which resorts to deceit. / Those members of an assembly who, having gone to an assembly, sit quietly meditating,
and do not speak according to the facts, are all speakers of falsehood; / and whoever, through desire, anger, or fear, does not state what was heard,
a thousand nooses of Varuṇa bind that man; / when a full year passes, one noose of these is released.
Therefore, the truth must be spoken directly by one who knows the truth.” / Hearing this, the ministers then said to Rāma:
“The owl is right, O king, not the vulture, O wise one! / You are the authority, O great king; indeed, the king is the ultimate refuge.
All subjects have the king as their root; the king is eternal dharma; / those men whose punisher is the king do not go to a bad state;
and released by Yama, they become best among men.” / Hearing the ministers’ words, Rāma spoke these words:
“Listen, I shall recount what is told in the Purāṇa: / heaven with its moon, sun, and constellations, along with mountains, earth, and trees,
the three worlds with moving and unmoving beings, submerged in an ocean of water, / was then truly singular, everything like a single sky.
Then the earth along with Lakṣmī entered Viṣṇu's belly; / holding her, the one of great splendour entered the ocean of water,
and having controlled his mind, he slept for many hundreds of years. / While Viṣṇu was asleep, Brahmā then entered his belly;
and knowing that it had many channels, the great yogin entered it. / From Viṣṇu's navel sprang a lotus adorned with gold.
Emerging from it, Brahmā, the great lord, becoming a yogin, / wishing to create the earth, the wind, the mountains, the trees,
all the subjects within them, humans, reptiles, / viviparous and oviparous creatures—he of great austerity created them all.
From his body arose Kaiṭabha along with Madhu; / those two demons, of great prowess and dreadful, had then obtained a boon.
Seeing Prajāpati there, both overwhelmed by anger, O king, / ran at the self-born lord with great speed in order to devour him.
Seeing all beings scattering separately in every direction, / Viṣṇu, praised by Brahmā, killed Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
and with their fat he increased the earth for its stability; / from the smell of their fat (medas), the earth received the name Medinī.
Therefore the vulture is untruthful; an evildoer, he makes another's dwelling / his own, being wicked-souled; he deserves punishment without doubt.”
Then a bodiless voice spoke from the sky: / “Do not kill the vulture, O Rāma, who was previously burnt by the power of asceticism!
"Long ago, O lord of people, ruler of men, this one was consumed by Gautama. / His name was Brahmadatta, a hero, true to his vows, pure.
Having come to the house of the brahmin sage, he begged for food; / and he ate there for a full hundred years, O best of kings.
Then, O king of great splendour, for this Brahmadatta he prepared water for the feet and the respectful offering, / indeed with his own hands, properly, for the sake of the meal.
Having entered that great-souled one's house for the meal, / he saw a woman with full breasts and then touched her with his hand.
Then a terrible curse was pronounced by the enraged sage: / 'Go into the state of a vulture, you fool!' The king then said to the sage:
'Have mercy, O most fortunate one; let there be deliverance from the curse!' / Hearing his words, the compassionate one spoke again, O ruler of men:
'In the lineage of Raghu will be born the highly renowned Rāma, / the highly fortunate lotus-eyed king of the Ikṣvākus.
Seen by him, you will be freed from sin, O bull among men.' / Having heard that, when seen by Rāma, he became the ruler of the earth.
Quickly casting off the state of a vulture, anointed with divine fragrant cosmetics, / this man of divine form addressed that ruler of men:
'Well done, O Rāghava, knower of dharma! Through your grace, O lord, / I am released from terrible hell, and indeed made free of sin by you.
The vulture's nature has been discarded by me, a ruler of the earth now in human form.' / The knower of dharma said to the owl: 'Enter your house, O Kauśika.
Having performed the twilight devotion, I will go where the sage is.' / Then, having touched water and performed the evening twilight devotion,
Rāma entered the hermitage of the great-souled pot-born sage. / Respectfully Agastya offered him very good fruits and roots
and savory vegetables to eat. / That tiger among men ate that food, which was like nectar.
Pleased and delighted, he stayed there for that night. / Having risen at dawn in the morning and performed his daily rites, O subduer of enemies,
The best of Raghu's line approached the sage in order to depart; / having greeted the great sage born of a pot, Rāma said:
'I take my leave; I depart, O brahmin; you should give me permission. / Blessed am I, favoured am I by the sight of you, O great sage.
And happily by your grace, great-souled one, I shall become a purified soul.' / While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking this wonderful speech,
the ascetic, supremely pleased, with tearful eyes, spoke: / 'Exceedingly wonderful is this speech of yours, O Rāma, of auspicious words,
purifying all beings, spoken by you, O delight of Raghu. / Those people who look upon you with friendship, O Rāma, even for a moment,
purified by all good hymns, are spoken of as dwellers in heaven. / And those living beings on earth who look upon you with fierce eyes,
slain by the staff of Brahmā, immediately go to hell. / Such are you, O best of Raghus, the purifier of all embodied beings.
And men who recount your glory will attain perfection, O Rāghava. / Go without distress, on an unobstructed path, with nothing to fear from any side.
Rule the kingdom with dharma, for you are the refuge of the worlds.' / Addressed thus by the sage, the king, with folded hands raised,
bowed to Agastya, the best of the sages. / Having bowed to that best of sages and to all those superior in asceticism,
he then, free from anxiety, mounted the Puṣpaka decorated with gold. / As he departed, the hosts of sages on all sides, with blessings,
honoured that king of men as the immortals honour the thousand-eyed Indra. / Then, when midday had arrived, Rāma, skilled in every matter,
Having reached Ayodhyā, the descendant of Kakutstha stepped down to the courtyard on foot; / then, having dismissed the radiant Puṣpaka [chariot] that moves at will,
stepping out from within the courtyard, the king said this to the doorkeepers: / 'Go with swift strides to Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata;
announcing my arrival, bring them without delay.' / Then, having heard the words of Rāma of untiring deeds, the doorkeepers,
having gone and summoned the two princes, announced them to Rāghava. / The two princes were brought by the doorkeepers at Rāghava's command.
Rāghava, seeing the beloved Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa arrived, / embraced them both, and Rāma spoke these words:
'Truly I have accomplished the unsurpassed work of the twice-born. / O two descendants of Raghu, I wish to perform further acts grounded in dharma.
"Together with you two, who are my own self, I wish to sacrifice / with the Rājasūya, the best of rites, wherein dharma is eternal."
Long ago, indeed, by Brahmā the creator of the worlds residing at Puṣkara, / three hundred and sixty sacrifices were performed.
Having sacrificed with the royal consecration sacrifice in accordance with dharma, Soma, knowing dharma, / obtained the unsurpassed place of fame in all the worlds.
Having sacrificed with the royal consecration sacrifice, Mitra, the destroyer of foes, / attained the state of Varuṇa at a truly auspicious moment.
Therefore, both of you reflect upon this matter and tell me what is beneficial.' / Bharata said: / 'You are supreme dharma, O virtuous one; in you all the earth
is established, O mighty-armed one of immeasurable prowess, and so is fame. / And all kings look upon you as the immortals look upon the lord of creatures,
O lord of the world, and so do we. / And the subjects, O king, look upon you like a father, O noble-minded one.
You are the refuge of living beings here on earth, O Rāghava. / You, therefore, should not perform such a sacrifice, O scorcher of enemies,
since the destruction of all beings on earth is seen [to follow it]. / It is heard, O tiger among kings, ruler of men, that in the case of Soma,
a very great battle of celestial bodies took place in the war on account of Tārā; / Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, was abducted by Soma out of lust.
In that, a great battle occurred, destroying gods and Dānavas. / In the terrible rite of Varuṇa, in battle, fish and tortoises,
all aquatic creatures perished, O tiger among kings, when it was over. / At the conclusion of Hariścandra's royal consecration sacrifice, O Rāghava,
the great Āḍībaka battle took place, destroying all the worlds. / Whatsoever creatures on earth belong to the animal species,
as well as celestial and earthly beings, destruction of them is heard to occur in a royal consecration sacrifice. / Therefore, O tiger among men, reflecting with your intellect, O king,
practise gentle, perfect dharma, beneficial to living beings.' / Having heard the words of Bharata, Rāghava said with respect:
'I am pleased with this speech of yours, O slayer of foes, knower of dharma! / My mind has turned away from the royal consecration sacrifice, O lover of dharma.
I shall practise complete dharma, and at Kānyakubja I will establish / Vāmana, O hero. My fame, gone to heaven,
will be established without doubt, as the Gaṅgā was by Bhagīratha.'

1.38.m: Bhīṣma said: / 'How was Vāmana installed at Kānyakubja by Rāma, O brahmin sage, / and where was he found? Proclaim it to me in detail.
For indeed sweet is this speech that is proclaimed concerning the praise of Rāma; / it has been uttered to me, O venerable one, bringing delight to the ear.
With affection people look upon that Rāghava out of love, / knowing dharma, grateful, and steadfast in wisdom.'
Deeply composed, he ruled the whole earth with dharma; / while he governed the realm, trees bore every desired fruit,
tasty and abundant, and varied garments [were produced]; / the earth brought forth crops without tilling, free of rivals for the great-souled one.
He accomplished the mission of the gods; Rāvaṇa, the thorn of the world, / together with his sons and ministers, was struck down merely in sport.
His mind became intent upon complete dharma, O best of the twice-born; / I desire to hear all his deeds, O sage.
Pulastya said: / But after some time, as Rāma stood upon the path of dharma, / hear with a focused mind, O king, O mighty-armed one, what he did.
He remembered the lord of the rakṣasas: “How is King Vibhīṣaṇa, / the rakṣasa established in Laṅkā, to rule his realm?
Hostility toward the gods is the mark of destruction; / but I granted him that kingdom to last as long as the moon and the sun.
Through his not perishing, my eternal renown will remain steadfast. / Rāvaṇa performed ascetic penance only for his own destruction here,
and that most sinful one has now been destroyed by me in the service of the gods. / Therefore, I must now go in person and seek out Vibhīṣaṇa.
What is beneficial to him must be instructed, so that he may endure eternally.” / While Rāma of boundless splendor was thinking thus,
Bharata arrived, saw Rāma, and spoke these words: / “What are you contemplating, my lord? Speak to me without secret,
whether regarding the gods' affairs, the earth, or your own purpose, O best of men.” / To Bharata who was speaking thus and waiting thoughtfully,
Rāghava spoke this word: “Indeed, there is no secret from you; / you are my external life-breath, as is the highly renowned Lakṣmaṇa.
There is nothing to be kept from you; know my truth. / This is my great concern: how does Vibhīṣaṇa fare among the gods,
for whose welfare indeed the Ten-Necked one was struck down? / Therefore, I shall go to Laṅkā where that Vibhīṣaṇa is.
And having seen that city and spoken the necessary task to that rakṣasa, / and having surveyed the whole earth, [seeing] Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys,
and the great king Śatrughna, and my brother's sons all around.” / While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, Bharata, standing before him,
spoke this word to Rāghava: “I shall go with you; / act thus, O mighty-armed one, and let Saumitri remain here.”
Having spoken thus to Bharata and Saumitri, Rāma indeed said: "In the city / protection must be maintained by you, O hero, until our return."
Having thus instructed Lakṣmaṇa and meditating upon the Puṣpaka [vimāna], O king, / he, the enhancer of Kausalyā's joy, boarded the aerial vehicle.
Then the Puṣpaka reached the region where the country of Gāndhāra lies; / seeing Bharata's two sons and observing the governance of the world,
and going from there to the eastern direction where Lakṣmaṇa's two sons were, / having stayed for six nights in those cities, the two descendants of Raghu
went by that vimāna toward the southern direction. / Having bowed to Bharadvāja at Prayāga, frequented by sages, where the Gaṅgā and Yamunā unite,
the two went to Atri's hermitage. / Having conversed with the sages there, they reached Janasthāna.
Rāma said: / “Here Sītā was formerly abducted by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, / having slain the vulture Jaṭāyus, who was indeed our father's friend.
Here occurred our great battle with the evil-minded Kabandha; / when slain and cremated by us, [he said]: ‘Sītā is in the abode of Rāvaṇa.
"On the excellent mountain Ṛṣyamūka is a monkey named Sugrīva; / he will render assistance to you. Go to Pampā with your younger brother."
Having reached Lake Pampā, approach the female ascetic Śabarī.’ / Addressed thus, sorrowful, O hero, I stood bereft of hope for life.
This is that lotus pool, O hero, on which Lakṣmaṇa spoke: / ‘Do not grieve, O tiger among men, destroyer of foes!
With me as your obedient servant, you will recover the princess of Mithilā.’ / Here indeed my rainy months passed like a hundred years.
Right here Vālin was slain for the sake of Sugrīva, O scorcher of foes; / surely this Kiṣkindhā, ruled by Vālin, is now visible,
wherein that virtuous monkey-king Sugrīva / dwells with the monkeys for a hundred years, O hero.”
Just as Sugrīva was sitting in the assembly together with the monkeys, / the two heroes, Bharata and the descendant of Raghu, arrived there in the city.
Seeing that the two brothers had arrived, he bowed low and spoke this: / “Where are the two of you heroes setting out for? What task are you going to do?”
Seating the two on a seat, he personally gave the guest-offerings then. / While the most righteous descendant of Raghu was thus seated in the assembly,
Aṅgada, Hanūmat, Nala, Nīla, Pāṭala, / Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, and the highly renowned Panasa,
priests, ministers, the astrologer Dadhivaktra, / Nīla, Śatabali, Mainda, Dvivida, Gandhamādana,
Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, Vīrasena, Vināyaka, / Sūryābha, Kumuda, and Suṣeṇa, commander of the monkey troops,
Ṛṣabha, Vinata, and Gavākṣa of terrible valor, / and the king of bears, Dhūmra, approached together with their armies.
All the inner chambers—Rumā, Tārā as well, / the women's quarters of Aṅgada, and other attendant women—
attaining peerless delight, exclaimed, “Excellent, excellent!” / And the noble monkeys, together with Sugrīva then,
and the highly fortunate monkey women led by Tārā, looking at Rāghava there, / their voices choked with tears, bowed down and spoke this:
“Where is that lady, my lord, whom, having completely conquered Rāvaṇa / and made her undergo purification in the fire before our father, the lord of Umā,
you brought to the city, O Rāma? We do not see her before you. / Without her, O lord, you do not shine, O descendant of Raghu!
Where does that virtuous Jānakī remain even without you? / We know of no other wife for you; bereft of a wife, you do not look resplendent,
like a pair of krauñca birds separated from one another, or a pair of cakravākas.” / To that Tārā, whose face resembled the lord of the stars, who was speaking thus,
Rāma, the lotus-eyed, best of the eloquent, said: / “O fair-toothed one, O wide-eyed lady, Time is indeed hard to overcome.
Know that this whole world of moving and unmoving beings is made by Time.” / Dismissing all those women, Sugrīva stood facing him.
Sugrīva said: / “For what purpose have you two lords of men come here? / Let that also be told quickly, for the time for action is here.”
As Sugrīva was speaking thus, Bharata, urged by Rāma, / described the departure of Rāghava to Laṅkā; / and Sugrīva said to the two: "Together with you two, to the city..."
I shall go to see the rakṣasa Vibhīṣaṇa there, O lord.” / When Sugrīva had spoken thus, Rāghava said: “Come along.”
Sugrīva and the two descendants of Raghu—the three of them stood in the Puṣpaka. / Then the vimāna reached the northern shore of the ocean.
Rāma spoke to Bharata: “Here indeed, for the sake of his life, Vibhīṣaṇa, / the lord of rakṣasas, arrived with four ministers.
Then he was consecrated in the sovereignty of Laṅkā by Lakṣmaṇa. / And here on this far shore of the ocean I stayed for three days [thinking]:
‘He will grant me an audience; the work of a kinsman will take place.’ / Yet so long no audience was granted to me by him, O slayer of foes.”
Then great anger arose in me on the fourth day, O Rāghava. / Having drawn my bow swiftly, a divine weapon was held in my hand.
Seeing me, seeking refuge and terrified, he took shelter with Lakṣmaṇa. / I was appeased by Sugrīva: 'May you forgive him, O Rāghava!'
Then the arrow loosed by me was turned away to the Maru region. / Thereupon, by the king of the ocean, who was exceedingly humble,
I was told: 'Go to Laṅkā by building a bridge, O Rāghava, / having crossed the great ocean filled with water, O tiger among men.'
This bridge was built by me across the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa; / within three days it was brought to completion by the best of monkeys.
On the first day, fourteen yojanas were constructed; / on the second day, thirty-six; and on the third, fifty.
Here that Laṅkā is seen, with golden ramparts and archways; / here a great siege was laid by the best of monkeys.
Here a great battle took place on the fourteenth day of the bright half of Caitra, / on the forty-eighth day, where that Rāvaṇa was slain.
Here Prahasta, the foremost of the Rākṣasas, was slain by Nīla; / and right here Dhūmrākṣa was struck down by Hanūmat.
Mahodara and Atikāya were slain by the high-souled Sugrīva; / right here Kumbhakarṇa was slain by me, and likewise Indrajit by Lakṣmaṇa.
And here the ten-necked one, the foremost of Rākṣasas, was slain by me. / Here Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived to converse with me,
along with the god who holds the trident, whose banner bears the bull, accompanied by Pārvatī; / the host of gods headed by Mahendra, together with Gandharvas and Kinnaras.
And my father, the great king, arrived from heaven, / surrounded by hosts of Apsarases and also by throngs of Vidyādharas.
In the presence of all of them, Sītā, desiring purification for the daughter of Janaka, / was addressed; she entered the sacrificial fire and attained purity.
Seen by the gods and the lord of Laṅkā, she was accepted at the command of my father. / Then I was addressed by the king: 'Go to Ayodhyā, my dear son.'
'Heaven is not valued by me without you, O Rāghava. / I have been redeemed by you, my son; I have attained the world of Indra.'
And the king said to Lakṣmaṇa: 'O son, merit has been earned by you; / together with your brother, you will attain the highest, divine worlds.'
Calling the daughter of Janaka, the king spoke this word: / 'No anger should be harbored by you toward your husband, O faithful one.'
'Eminent fame indeed will belong to your husband, O fair-eyed one.' / While Rāma was speaking thus, seated in the Puṣpaka vimāna,
the excellent Rākṣasas there quickly went to Vibhīṣaṇa. / The spies spoke thus at that time: 'Rāma has arrived with Sugrīva.'
Vibhīṣaṇa, upon hearing of Rāma's arrival nearby, / honored those spies with all desirable things, wealth, and the like.
Adorning that city, he went out with his ministers. / Seeing Rāma stationed in the aerial car, like the sun on Mount Meru,
bowing down with an eight-limbed prostration, he said to Rāghava: / 'Today my birth has borne fruit; all my desires have been attained,'
Since your divine feet have been seen, worshipful by the world and blameless, / I have been made worthy of praise, O lord, by the sky-dwellers headed by Śakra.
'I consider myself greater than Purandara, the lord of the gods.' / In the radiant palace of Rāvaṇa, adorned with all jewels,
when the descendant of Kakutstha was seated, Vibhīṣaṇa offered the arghya / and, joining his palms, spoke to Sugrīva and Bharata:
'Whatever I can give to Rāma who has come here, I possess that not. / This Laṅkā, by slaying the sinful enemy who was a thorn to the three worlds,
was previously given to me as my city by Rāma. / This city, these wives, these sons, and myself—
all this is given by me; may it all be imperishable for you.' / Then all the subjects and the inhabitants living in Laṅkā
came, filled with curiosity, to see Rāghava. / Vibhīṣaṇa was addressed by them: 'O lord, show us Rāma.'
It was told by Vibhīṣaṇa to the high-souled Rāghava. / Urged by Rāma, Bharata and the lord of monkeys
accepted all their gifts, the mass of collected wealth and jewels. / Thus Rāma lived there for three days in the home of the Rākṣasa.
When the fourth day arrived and Rāma was seated in the assembly, / Kekasī said this to her son: 'O son, I wish to see Rāma.'
'When he is seen, great merit is obtained by the best of sages. / He is the eternal Viṣṇu of four forms, the highly fortunate one.'
'Sītā is Lakṣmī, O highly fortunate one; she was not recognized by your elder brother. / Formerly, at an assembly of gods in heaven, it was told by your father:'
'Viṣṇu indeed will become the son of Daśaratha in the family of the Raghus, / for the destruction of the ten-necked Rākṣasa.'
Vibhīṣaṇa said: / 'Do so indeed, mother; take a new garment / and a vessel containing sandalwood together with curds, honey, and unbroken grains of rice.'
'Offer the arghya with dūrvā grass upon seeing the prince. / Placing Saramā in front, as well as the other maiden daughters of the gods,'
'go to the presence of Rāghava; therefore, I will go ahead.' / Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasa went to where Rāma was seated.
Clearing away all the Dānavas who had assembled to see Rāma, / having made that assembly immaculate, [he saw] Rāma seated facing him.
Vibhīṣaṇa said: / 'O lord, ruler of the people, hear what is to be submitted as I speak: / she who gave birth to the ten-necked one, to Kumbhakarṇa, and to me—'
'here is that mother of ours, O lord; she desires to see your feet. / Taking compassion on her, you ought to grant her an audience.'
Rāma said: / 'Desiring to see a mother, I shall go / near to her, O king of Rākṣasas; go quickly before me.'
Having consented to that word, the Lord arose from the excellent seat, / and placing his joined palms upon his head, he made a bow:
'I salute you; you are a mother according to dharma, / through your great asceticism and diverse merits.'
'If a mortal sees these two feet of yours, O goddess, / he will be fulfilled; so I am delighted having seen these two, O you who are affectionate toward sons.'
'Just as Kausalyā is my mother, so too are you mine.' / And Kekasī said to Rāma: 'Live long, be happy!'
'It was told to me by my husband, O hero: Viṣṇu, assuming a human form, / has descended into the family of Raghu for the welfare of the gods here,'
'for the destruction of the ten-necked one, to grant prosperity to Vibhīṣaṇa, / the killing of Vālin, and the building of the bridge across the ocean.'
'The son of Daśaratha will accomplish all that.' / Now you are recognized by me, recalling that which was spoken by my husband.
Sītā is Lakṣmī, you are Viṣṇu, and the monkeys are indeed gods. / I shall go home, my son; attain enduring fame!'
Saramā said: / 'Remaining in the Aśoka grove for a full year right here, / the daughter of Janaka was attended upon, O lord; may your beloved dwell in comfort.'
'O scorcher of foes, I constantly remember the two feet of Sītā; / pondering day and night: "When shall I see that queen?"'
'Why was the daughter of Janaka not brought here by the god of gods? / Alone, without that woman, you do not shine at all.'
'Sītā shines beside you, and you beside her, O scorcher of foes.' / While she was speaking thus, Bharata said these words: 'Who is this?'

Then Rāma, who understood intentions, smiled and quickly said to Bharata:
"She is indeed the wife of Vibhīṣaṇa, Saramā by name.

She is considered a very firm and noble dear friend of Sītā.
Seeing that everything is caused by time, I do not know what she will do.

Go, fortunate woman! Guard your husband's home, beautiful lady!
Leaving me, the queen has gone, just as good fortune deserts the unfortunate.

Deprived of her, O fair-browed one, I shall never find delight.
I see all directions as completely empty as I wander here again."

And Saramā, the dear friend of Sītā, was dismissed.
Then, when the Kekaya woman had departed, Rāma addressed Vibhīṣaṇa:
“What is pleasing to the gods must be done; no offense should be committed by you against the deities. / By the command of the king of kings you should act, O sinless one."
“If any human should come to Laṅkā by any means, / he must not be killed by the rākṣasas; he is to be regarded just as I am.”
Vibhīṣaṇa said: / “By your command, O tiger among men, I will do all of this.” / While Vibhīṣaṇa was speaking thus, Vāyu spoke to Rāma:
“Here is an image of Viṣṇu, by which Bali was formerly bound; / take it, O fortunate one, and install it in Kānyakubja.”
Knowing that intention declared by Vāyu, / Vibhīṣaṇa, having adorned Vāmana with all kinds of jewels,
brought [it] and offered [it] to Rāma, and spoke these words: / “When Śakra was defeated by Meghanāda, O Rāghava,
then indeed this Vāmana was brought here, O lotus-eyed one. / Take this god of gods, and install the god of gods.”
Saying “So be it,” Rāghava mounted the Puṣpaka, / [taking] immeasurable wealth, jewels, and Vāmana, the highest of the gods.
Taking [them], Sugrīva and Bharata mounted after Vāmana. / Moving in the sky, Rāma said to Vibhīṣaṇa, “Halt!”
Hearing the word of Rāghava, he in turn said to Rāghava: / “I will do all this indeed that has been commanded by you, O lord.
By this causeway, O king of kings, all men on earth / might come and cause affliction, and your command would be violated.
What is my rule here, O god? What indeed should be done by me, O lord?” / Hearing these words spoken by the best of rākṣasas,
Rāma took the bow in hand and cut the causeway in two; / and dividing it swiftly into three parts, in the middle indeed for ten yojanas,
and cutting one yojana and another, three segments were made. / Reaching the coastal forest, Rāma [performed] the worship of the lord of Ramā,
having consecrated Janārdana, the god of gods, by the name of Rāmeśvara; / then, taking Vāmana, the delight of the Raghus
departed in haste from the southern ocean. / From the sky came a voice deep as a thundercloud.
Rudra said: / “Hail, O Rāma, may good fortune be yours! I am situated here now; / as long as this world remains, O Rāma, as long as this earth endures,
so long shall your causeway remain as a sacred ford, O Rāghava.” / Having heard such nectar-like speech of the god of gods,
Rāma said: / “Salutations to you, O lord of the gods, granter of fearlessness to devotees! / O beloved of Gaurī, salutations to you, destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice!
Salutations to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the boon-giver; / always to the lord of beasts, to the fierce one, and to the matted-haired one;
to Mahādeva, to the terrible one, to Tryambaka, to the lord of the directions; / to Īśāna, to the slayer of Bhaga; salutations to the slayer of Andhaka;
to the blue-necked one, to the dreadful one, to the creator praised by the Creator; / to the slayer of Kumāra's enemies, and to the begetter of Kumāra;
to the deep red one, to the smoke-colored one, to Śiva, and to the slayer; / salutations to the one with the blue crest, to the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of Daityas;
to the fierce one, to the three-eyed one, whose seed is gold and fire; / to the blameless one, husband of Ambikā, praised by all the gods;
to the accessible, to the desirable, salutations indeed to Sadyojāta; / to the bull-bannered one, to the shaven-headed one, to the one with matted locks, to the celibate student;
to the one undergoing tapas, to the object of tapas, to the patron of brahmins, and to victory; / to the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe, who stands pervading the universe!
Salutations, salutations to the divine one, the remover of the distress of the surrendered; / to the one compassionate to devotees, O god, who reside in the mind as the light of the universe!”
Pulastya said: / Being praised thus, Hara, the god of gods, O king, / spoke words to Rāghava, who stood before him bowed in devotion.
Rudra said: / “Hail, O Rāghava, may good fortune be yours! Speak what is in your mind. / You are surely Nārāyaṇa, concealed within human wombs,
incarnated; and that mission of the gods has been accomplished by you, O sinless one. / Now go to your own abode; you have accomplished your task, O slayer of foes.
A supreme sacred ford has been made by you named the Causeway, O delight of the Raghus. / Coming here to the ocean, men, O king, shall see it;
those laden with great sins—their sin dissolves away. / Sins such as the murder of a brahmin, whatever severe ones there may be,
are destroyed merely by seeing it; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. / Go, having installed Vāmana on the bank of the Gaṅgā, O best of Raghus,
having divided the earth in all ways into eight parts, O scorcher of foes; / go to Śvetadvīpa, your own abode, O god! Salutations to you.”
Then, having bowed, Rāma reached the sacred ford of Puṣkara. / But the celestial chariot would not go upward, encircled; then Rāghava [said]:
“Why is this vehicle held fast, stationary in the sky without support? / There must be a reason; look!” he said to the monkey.
Sugrīva, descending to the surface of the earth at Rāma's word, / saw Brahmā accompanied by the gods and the Siddhas,
accompanied by the host of brahmin seers, attended by the four Vedas. / Having seen him, he came and said to Rāma: “The grandfather of all the worlds,
accompanied by the world-guardians, and by the hosts of the Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts [is here]; / the Puṣpaka indeed cannot overstep that divine Grandfather.”
Descending then from the gold-adorned Puṣpaka, Rāma, / having bowed to the god Viriñcana seated with Gāyatrī,
by prostrating with eight limbs, touching the earth with five limbs, / having bowed down, praised Viriñcana, the god of gods.
Rāma said: / “I bow to the creator of the world, honored by Prajāpatis and gods, / lord of the gods, lord of the world, lord of creatures, master of the universe.
Salutations to you, god of the gods, revered by gods and asuras, / lord of past, future, and present, with eyes tawny-yellow like Hari's.
You are a child and you have the form of an old man, with an antelope skin as your seat and garment; / you are the savior and the god, you are the master and ruler of the three worlds.
The golden-wombed, lotus-wombed, Veda-wombed, giver of traditional law, / the great adept, the one with the great lotus, bearing a great staff, wearing a girdle;
time and having the form of time, blue-necked, best of the wise, / author of the Vedas, eternal child, imperishable lord of beasts;
holding darbha grass in hand, with a swan on your banner, creator, destroyer, Hara, Hari, / matted-haired, bald, tufted, staff-bearing, holding a club, of great renown;
lord of beings, overseer of the gods, self of all, source of all, / omnipresent, destroyer of all, creator, and imperishable guru;
the god bearing a water-pot, and likewise holding the sacrificial ladles sruk and sruva, / worthy of offering, worthy of worship, the syllable Om, singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman;
death and also immortality, Pāriyātra, observing good vows, / celibate student, keeper of vows, cave-dweller, of lovely lotuses;
immortal, handsome to behold, resembling the morning sun, / attended on the right and on the left by your two wives;
a mendicant, having the form of a mendicant, with three braids of matted hair, of resolute conviction, / prompter of mental thoughts, desire, spring, and the honey-bee;
forest hermit, dweller in the woods, belonging to an āśrama, worshipped, / supporter of the universe and maker, the eternal and immovable spirit;
overseer of dharma, diverse-eyed, of threefold dharma, source of beings, / possessing three Vedas, multiform, with radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
the deluder and the binder, especially of the Dānavas; / god of gods, marked with lotuses, three-eyed, with lotus matted locks.”

He had a tawny beard, held a bow, was formidable, and had the prowess of dharma.
Thus praised by Rāma, Brahmā, the best of the knowers of Brahman,

taking bowing Rāma by the hand, the grandfather said:
"You are Viṣṇu, descended in a human body upon the surface of the earth.

All that divine task has been accomplished by you, O great lord!
Having installed the god Vāmana on the southern bank of the Jāhnavī,

and having gone to your own city Ayodhyā, go to the world of the gods."
Dismissed by Brahmā, Rāma bowed down to the grandfather,

mounted the Puṣpaka vehicle, and reached the city of Madhurā.
Having seen Śatrughna, the slayer of foes, together with his son,

the glorious Rāghava, Bharata, and the lord of monkeys rejoiced.
Śatrughna, [seeing] his two brothers arrived like Śakra and Upendra,

then bowed with his head, embracing the earth with his five limbs.
Rāma, lifting up his brother, quickly placed him on his lap.

Then after him Bharata [did so], and immediately after him Sugrīva.
Then, having quickly taken the guest-offering for Rāma as he sat,

he offered the kingdom and prostrated with eight limbs before Rāghava then.
Having heard that Rāma had arrived, all the people of Mathurā,

the castes, consisting predominantly of brāhmaṇas, came together to see him.
Having conversed with all the subjects, the citizens along with the brāhmaṇas,

and having dwelt there for five days, Rāma set his mind upon leaving.
And then Śatrughna brought horses and elephants to Rāma,

as well as fashioned and unworked gold there as a gift.
Then Rāma, pleased, said: "All this has been given by me to you;

anoint your two sons as kings over the people of Mathurā."
Having spoken thus, Rāma then, when the sun had reached midday,

reached Mahodaya on the bank of the Gaṅgā, installed Vāmana,
and said to the twice-born and also to future kings:

"This bridge of dharma, which increases prosperity, has been made by me.
When the time comes, it must be protected and never destroyed in any way.

Thus with outstretched hand this prayer is made by me:
O kings, my request having been made, let protection be carried out here!

Daily worship must be performed by all, unflagging,
having granted villages and that wealth which was brought from Laṅkā."

And having sent Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, to Kiṣkindhā,
Rāma went to Ayodhyā and then said to that Puṣpaka:

"You must not come again; stay where the lord of wealth is."
Having accomplished his purpose, Rāma then considered that nothing remained to be done.

Pulastya said:
"Thus, O king Bhīṣma, in connection with the story of Rāma,
the manifestation of Vāmana has been told to you. What more do you wish to hear?

I shall tell all that wherein your curiosity lies, O king;
I will declare all to you that you desire, O delight of kings."

1.39.m:
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus indeed the glorification of Vāmana has been told at length.
Now tell me further the other glorification of that Viṣṇu.

How was the lotus on the navel of the god, from which the world arose?
And how did the Vaiṣṇava creation take place formerly in the middle of the lotus?

How did the world become composed of lotuses in the great Pādma kalpa?
How was that which is born in the waters produced on the navel of him who rested upon the ocean of waters?
The majesty of Padmanābha sleeping on the ocean waters, / and how the gods and the hosts of sages arose in ancient times at Puṣkara—

Declare this entirely, O lord of those who know yoga, the yoga
by which he fashioned this eternal world there.

How, when there was a single desolate ocean, when the moving and unmoving had perished,
when the terrestrial globe was burned, and serpents and rākṣasas were destroyed,

when fire, wind, and space were destroyed, when dharma was destroyed on the surface of the earth,
when it had become a mere abyss, during the dissolution of the great elements,

did the lord of the universe Himself, of great splendour and immense brilliance,
remain fixed in meditation, resorting to proper order as a master of yoga?

To me listening with supreme devotion, O brāhmaṇa, you ought
to speak this without remainder, O knower of dharma, the glory whose essence is Nārāyaṇa.

To me, full of faith and seated properly, O venerable one, you ought to speak."
Pulastya said:
"Since you have a desire to hear the fame of Nārāyaṇa,
[this is] fitting for you, purified by noble lineage and descent, O scion of the Kuru race! / Hear as it is told in the ancient Purāṇas and from the gods according to the Veda.

and having heard from the speaking brāhmaṇas, who are very great souls,
and as the glorious son of Parāśara, the teacher Dvaipāyana, who equals Bṛhaspati in splendour,

having seen it by penance, declared it—that I shall tell you
according to my devotion and according to what has been heard,

as it was properly understood by me through the path of the sages, O best of men.
Who can venture to know the Supreme whose nature is Nārāyaṇa?

Even Brahmā does not truly know this descent of the universe.
His deed belongs to all the gods; it is a secret among the great sages.

He is the object of worship in all sacrifices; He is reality for the seers of reality,
the inner self for the knowers of the inner self, and hell for evil-doers.

He is the presiding deity and that deity called the presiding divinity;
He is the primary element and that element, and the supreme for seekers of the supreme goal.

He is the sacrifice taught in the Vedas; poets know Him as that asceticism.
He who is the agent, the instrument, the intellect, and from whom comes the knower of the field,

the syllable Om, the Puruṣa, the ruler, and He is conceived as the One,
as the fivefold breath of life, the firm, and the imperishable.

He is called Time, maturity, sacrifice, the sacrificer, and study;
He is spoken of through diverse states, yet He is that Supreme.

That Lord alone does everything and does nothing.
He causes everything to be done in this [world], and the work of those who abide is done [by Him].

We sacrifice to Him alone, the Primal One; He alone is delighted by the rising.
He who is the speaker, that which is to be spoken, and that which I speak to you,

that which is heard, that which is to be heard, and whatever else is chattered,
whatever discourse, whatever scriptures, whoever is righteous and intent upon righteousness,

the universe, and whoever is the lord of the universe—He is traditionally known as Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever is true, whatever is false, what is beginning, middle, and end, what is limitless, and what will be,

whatever moves or does not move, whatever else exists—all that is the supreme Puruṣa, the primary entity.
They say that the Kṛta age consists of four thousand years.

Its twilight is as many hundreds doubled, O delight of the Kurus,
wherein dharma has four feet, while adharma has one foot as its body;

wherein humans are born peaceful and devoted to their own duties,
the brāhmaṇas abide intent on dharma, and kings abide in the conduct of kings.
The vaiśyas are dedicated to agriculture, and the śūdras likewise to service; / then truthfulness, goodness, and dharma flourish.
Dharma is practiced by the virtuous, by which the world is sustained. / This was the conduct in the Kṛta age of all creatures, O king,
of living beings known for righteousness, of men, and of those of low birth. / Three thousand years are here said to be the Tretā age.
Its twilight is declared to be of that many hundred [years], doubled [for the dawn and dusk]. / Adharma stands on two feet, and dharma is established on three.
Where truth, goodness, and the rites of dharma are performed, / [yet] in the Tretā the castes undergo corruption, being filled with greed.
Degradation of the four castes, tolerance, and indeed weakness— / this is the course of the Tretā yuga, wondrous and fashioned by the gods.
The Dvāpara yuga lasts for two thousand years, O delight of the Kurus; / its twilight is as many hundred years; twice that is called the yuga.
There too living beings are exceedingly bent on wealth, overcome by passion; / rogues, deceivers, and vile persons are born, O delight of the Kurus.
Dharma stands upon two feet, while adharma has risen upon three; / through hundreds of reversals, dharma goes to destruction in the Kali age.
Devotion to the Veda falls away, and belief in the hereafter is abandoned; / vows and fasts are forsaken in the Kali yuga, at the turn of the cosmic age.
Then its measure is one thousand years, and also two hundred years, / in which adharma possesses four quarters and dharma takes but a single quarter.
Where human beings are born lustful, false ascetics, and base; / no one is resolute, none is virtuous, and none speaks the truth.
Men there are known as atheists, unfaithful to brāhmaṇas, / seized by egotism, with the bonds of affection shattered.
All brāhmaṇas follow the conduct of śūdras in the Kali yuga; / a reversal of the stages of life prevails in the Kali yuga.
There is confusion among the castes at the end of the yuga, O delight of the Kurus. / This cycle called twelve thousand years was fashioned in the beginning.
A period lasting a thousand yugas is called a day of Brahmā. / Then, when that day has passed, for all living beings,
seeing the dissolution of their bodies, Time, possessing the intellect of destruction, / of all the gods and the brāhmaṇas, O king,
of the daityas and the dānavas, of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and birds, / of gandharvas, apsarases, and serpents, O ruler of the earth,
of mountains, rivers, and beasts, O best of men, / and of those who have entered animal wombs, of worms and biting insects—
the lord of all beings, having become the five elements, the creator of beings, / performs a great slaughter for the sake of withdrawing the universe.

Becoming the sun, taking away their two eyes; becoming the wind, [taking away] the swarm of living beings' breaths; / becoming fire, burning all the worlds; becoming a cloud, he violently rained upon them again.
Having become the yogin Nārāyaṇa, the all-formed fire, / he dries up the oceans with blazing rays.
Then, having drunk all the oceans, rivers, and wells from every side, / and drawing in all the water of the mountains, the knower of yoga,
having become the thousand-rayed sun, splitting the earth into the netherworld, / delights, drawing in the water and drinking the unsurpassed liquid.
Whatever is formed and unformed, and whatever else is enduring in living beings, / the lotus-eyed supreme spirit takes up all of that.
Having become a mighty wind, shaking the entire universe, / having reached the inward and outward breaths, Hari advances with the wind.
Then, of the multitudes of gods and of all embodied beings, / all the qualities of the five senses and whatever elements there are—
the smellable, the smell, and the body: these qualities resting on the earth; / the course of the world is destroyed by the Blessed Lord in a moment.
The tongue, taste, and moisture: the qualities resting in water; / form, the eye, and distinction: the qualities resting in the light of the eyes;
touch, breath, and motion: the qualities resting in the wind; / sound, both ears, and hearing: the qualities resting in the sky;
the mind, intellect, and consciousness, resting in the knower of the field; / and Parameṣṭhin, along with the highest, has taken refuge in Hṛṣīkeśa.
Then, enveloped by the rays of that Blessed Lord / and driven by the wind, they settled upon the branches of the earth.
Arising from their withdrawal, the fire, blazing in a hundred ways, / burning up the entire universe, became the fire of cosmic dissolution.
Mountains, trees, bushes, creepers, vines, and grasses, / celestial chariots, and various cities,
and whatever things served as shelters, it burned exceedingly. / Having reduced all those worlds to ashes, the teacher of the world's teacher,
he bore the ashes that arose from the worlds at the end of the yuga. / Becoming a great dark cloud with a thousand showers in a hundred ways,
he satisfied the earth with celestial water as an oblation. / Then, with sweet, supreme water resembling milk,
cool and pure, the earth attained pacification. / Blended with that water, the earth, through having the nature of milk,
became the waters of a single ocean, devoid of all living beings; / even the great creatures entered the all-pervading lord of unmeasured splendor.
When the sun, wind, and sky were gone, and the subtle universe was enclosed, / having himself brought about the drying up of the oceans and embodied beings,
having burned and contracted [them], the eternal one sleeps alone; / assuming his ancient form, the one of unmeasured stride sleeps.
Traveling on the water of the single ocean, the yogin absorbed in yoga / for many thousands of yugas in the water of the single ocean.
Neither the unmanifest nor the manifest is able to know / what the name of this spirit is, what the yoga is, and who possesses the yoga.
Neither behind, nor all around, nor at his side, nor in front / is anything discerned of him; the best of gods is seen.

Sky, earth, wind, waters, light, the lord of creatures, the supporter of the world, the lord of gods, / the grandfather, the resting-place of the Vedas, the sage—bringing all to an end, the powerful lord chose to sleep.
When the world had thus become a single ocean, the one of great splendor sleeps; / covering the earth with water, the swan acts as Nārāyaṇa.
In the midst of the great dust resembling the great ocean, / the lotus-eyed, mighty-armed one is what they know as the imperishable Brahman.
Surrounded by darkness having the same form as his own nature, the Lord, / taking up a sattvic mind wherein that sattva was placed,
then [imparted] true, supreme knowledge to Brahmā who had come to be, / and the secret was declared just as it is remembered in the Upaniṣads.
The Puruṣa is the sacrifice: this is celebrated as the highest; / and whichever other person is spoken of, he alone is the Supreme Puruṣa.
And the brāhmaṇas who perform sacrifices, who are remembered as officiating priests, / arose in the beginning from this very source, from the mouths, as is heard.
The Lord created the Brahmā priest first from his mouth, and the singing Udgātṛ priest; / and from his arms he created the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu priest;
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin alongside the Brahmā, and all the Stotṛs; / from his penis the Maitrāvaruṇa and the Pratiṣṭhātṛ;
from his belly the Pratihartṛ and the Potṛ, O king; / from his two hands the Āgnīdhra and the Yajur-reciting Unnetṛ;
from his two thighs the Acchāvāka and the Sāman-chanting Subrahmaṇya. / In this very way the Blessed Lord, the master of the world,
the self-existent one, created these sixteen excellent sacrificial priests for all sacrifices. / And then this great yogin, the Puruṣa known as sacrifice,
and all the Vedas, together with the limbs, the Upaniṣads, and the rituals, / sleeps in the single ocean, which was a wonder in ancient times.
Hear now: at that time, out of curiosity, the brāhmaṇa Mārkaṇḍeya, / that great sage, was swallowed by that Blessed Lord and lived in his belly.
Living for many thousands of years by the supreme splendor of that very Lord, / wandering through holy bathing-places across the earth, the range of holy places,
holy hermitages, and temples of the gods, / various regions, diverse kingdoms, and cities,
They are devoted to muttered prayer and oblation, tranquil, and remembered as pure through austerities. / Then Mārkaṇḍeya slowly emerged from his mouth.
Through the divine māyā, he did not know himself to be coming out. / Having emerged from his belly, then [he saw] the world as a single ocean,
and Mārkaṇḍeya beheld it covered on all sides by darkness. / An intense fear arose in him, and the reversal of his own life.
Gladdened by the sight of the god, he attained the utmost wonder. / He, unerring in soul, reflected; then Mārkaṇḍeya became anxious:
"Could it be a delusion of the mind, or is it a dream that is experienced? / Clearly, one of these two states must be mine.
For this is indeed no dream, connected with truth as truth deserves. / The moon, sun, and wind have perished; the mountains and earth have vanished.
Which world might this be?" Having thus fallen into sorrow, / he also saw a person sleeping, like a mountain,
