sunken, as it were, down in the water like a cloud in the ocean, / blazing as if with brilliance, wearing the moon and sun,
like the ocean in depth, shining with wondrous splendor. / "Having come here to behold the god, who are you?" he [asked] in wonder.
And just so, the sage was made to enter the belly once again. / Having entered the belly again, Mārkaṇḍeya, full of wonder,
recognizing once more the vision of the dream just as it was before, / wandered, just as before, over the earth and the forest,
abounding in holy sacred fords and various hermitages, / and [he saw] those sacrificing with rites, their priestly fees fully paid to the gurus.
He saw hundreds of twice-born men engaged in sacrifice, situated within the belly of the god, / all the castes, beginning with the brahmins, adhering to righteous conduct.
The four stages of life were properly observed, just as before. / In this way, for more than a hundred years, wise Mārkaṇḍeya,
wandering through the entire earth, observed [it all] within his belly. / Then, at some time, he emerged once again from the belly.
Having seen a single child sleeping on a branch of a banyan tree, / likewise in the waters of the single ocean, within [a space] enveloped by mist,
in a world where the unmanifest sported, devoid of all beings, / that sage, overcome with astonishment, was seized with curiosity.
He was unable to look upon the child, who resembled the sun. / Standing in solitude near the water, he also reflected,
he thought this had been seen before, bewildered by the divine māyā. / Mārkaṇḍeya, full of wonder, [saw him] lying on the fathomless water.
As before, he went to see him, with trembling eyes. / Then the Blessed One said to him: "Welcome, child!"
The Supreme Person spoke in a voice like a cloud: / "Mārkaṇḍeya, do not be afraid; come near me!"
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / "Who calls me by name, showing me disrespect, / and thus assails me, whose lifespan is named as a thousand divine years?
For even among the gods, this is not proper conduct toward me. / Even Brahmā speaks to me with affection, saying, 'O long-lived one!'
Who has forsaken his life today by confronting my terrible ascetic power? / Having addressed me as 'Mārkaṇḍeya,' you deserve to behold death!"
When the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya was thus agitated with anger, / then the Blessed One, the slayer of Madhu, spoke to him again.
The Blessed Lord said: / "I am your progenitor, my child, Hṛṣīkeśa, your father and guru, / the ancient giver of life. Why do you not approach me?
Long ago, desiring a son, your father, the sage of the lineage of Aṅgiras, / previously worshipped me, resorting to severe tapas.
Seeing him performing terrible tapas, with a splendor surpassing the thirty [gods], / I granted you as a son, a great sage of boundless splendor.
And who else has the power to behold me, the yogin consisting of the self of all beings, / resting in the single ocean, sporting by means of yoga-māyā?"
Then, his heart delighted and his eyes wide with wonder, / folding his hands in reverence at his head, Mārkaṇḍeya of great tapas,
announcing his name and lineage, the long-lived one honored by the world, / made obeisance with devotion to that Blessed One.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / "I wish to know this māyā of yours in its true nature, O sinless one, / whereby, remaining in the midst of the single ocean, you lie in the form of a child.
And by what name are you known in the world, O Lord? / I surmise you to be the Great Self; for who else could remain [thus]?"
The Blessed Lord said: / "I am Nārāyaṇa, O brahmin, the destroyer of all beings; / I have a thousand heads and mouths, and am endowed with a thousand feet.
I am the sun-colored Person, and in my mouth I consist of Brahmā; / I am Agni, the carrier of oblations, accompanied by the seven horses.
I am Śakra of the office of Indra; of the seasons, [I am] the cyclical year; / among yogins, I am known as Sāṃkhya; and [I am] the dissolution-cycle at the end of the ages.
I am all beings and all deities; / among serpents I am Śeṣa, and I am Tārkṣya among all birds.
I am Kṛtānta of all beings, known by the name of Time; / I am dharma and I am tapas for the dwellers of all stages of life.
I am compassion, the supreme duty; I am the Milk Ocean, the great sea. / What is true and one supreme reality—I alone am Prajāpati.
I am Sāṃkhya, I am Yoga, and I am that supreme state; / I am sacrifice, and I am the rite; I am remembered as the lord of knowledge.
I am light, I am wind, I am earth, I am water; / I am space, the oceans, the lunar mansions, and the ten directions.
I am rain, I am Soma, I am Parjanya, and I am the sun; / I am the supreme Purāṇa, and likewise I am the ultimate refuge.
And in the future I shall be everywhere, the summation of all that will be. / Whatever you see, O brahmin, and whatever you hear,
and whatever you experience in the world, remember all that as me. / The universe was created by me in the past; behold me as creating it even now.
And age after age I protect the entire world, O Mārkaṇḍeya. / All this has been told to you; understand it, O Mārkaṇḍeya!
Even while desiring to attend to the dharmas, wander happily in my belly! / Brahmā resides in my body, and the gods along with the sages.
Know me, the manifest and the unmanifest yoga, the enemy of Mura; / I am the single-syllabled mantra, and the three-syllabled grandfather.
Beyond the three aims of life is the oṃkāra, revealing the Supreme Self; / and thus the Ādipurāṇa speaks of me, O wise one."
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya entered the mouth of the Blessed One; / then the best of sages entered the belly of the Blessed One.

Facing him directly in solitude, wishing to hear from the imperishable Haṃsa,
who resorted to that manifold, undecaying state in the great ocean when moon and sun were gone,

moving slowly, the Lord then named Haṃsa, creating the world, wandered as time revolved.
And then, having thus purified himself, he surely chose asceticism,

covering his body with water, the lotus-born [Lord].
Then that great-souled one, exceedingly mighty, when releasing the mortal world,

thought of the universe for the great elements, he the universal [Lord].
While he was contemplating, the ocean having been firmly established,

the space-less, watery, subtle universe having dissolved,
the Lord entered the water and agitated the ocean.

Then within the waters an opening, subtle indeed, previously appeared;
then wind, possessing sound, arose from that opening.

Having obtained inner commotion, the wind grew;
by the forceful wind, the ocean was violently agitated.

From that agitated ocean, churned in those waters,
the black-pathed one arose—the great Lord Vaiśvānara [Fire].

Then the fire dried up much water;
the entire ocean became an opening, the vast sky.

Holy waters, resembling the essence of nectar, arose from his own brilliance;
the sky arose from the opening, and the wind arose from the sky.

Then seeing fire, born from friction and produced from his mouth,
the god, the Grandfather [Brahmā], the manifestor of the gross elements,

seeing the elements, the blessed one of manifold forms contemplated,
for the excellent creation of the worlds, together with the birth of Brahmā.

A thousand sets of four yugas are reckoned at the revolution of an age,
which belongs to the best of twice-born on earth whose minds are cultivated by tapas.

Having a soul purified through many births, Hari is proclaimed as Brahmā;
and the Soul of all, seeing their knowledge, attains suitability for yogis.

Knowing him possessed of yoga and complete, supreme sovereignty,
the knower of yoga appointed him to the universal station of Brahmā.

Then in those great waters, the Great Lord, Hari, Acyuta,
the maker of all worlds, properly engaged in water sport.

He then produced a single lotus originating from his navel,
thousand-hued, stainless, shining like the sun, and made of gold.

It rose with radiant splendour like the blazing flame of a fire, possessing the brilliance of the spotless autumn sun;
the noble, luminous lotus shone, its moss the beautiful body-hairs of the Great Soul.
